A.explanation: One antinode would need only $15 \text{ cm}$ for $\lambda = 30 \text{ cm}$, which is much shorter than the $45 \text{ cm}$ gap.

B.explanation: Two antinodes would need $30 \text{ cm}$ for $\lambda = 30 \text{ cm}$, which underestimates the $45 \text{ cm}$ separation.

C.explanation: With $\lambda = 30 \text{ cm}$, $45 \text{ cm}$ holds three half-wavelengths, giving three antinodes between the two nodes.

D.explanation: Four antinodes would need $60 \text{ cm}$ for $\lambda = 30 \text{ cm}$, which is longer than the $45 \text{ cm}$ available.

hints: Notice the $45 \text{ cm}$ separation has a node at each end, so its length must contain a whole number of half-wavelengths $\lambda/2$.
Calculate the wavelength from the $1.00 \text{ GHz}$ frequency using $\lambda = c/f$ with $c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Compare $45 \text{ cm}$ with your $\lambda/2$ value to find how many half-wavelength loops fit, recalling each loop contains one antinode.
walkthrough: Find the wavelength of the microwaves using $c = f\lambda$. Here $f = 1.00 \text{ GHz} = 1.00 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$.
Rearrange and substitute: $\lambda = c/f = (3.00 \times 10^8)/(1.00 \times 10^9) = 0.30 \text{ m} = 30 \text{ cm}$.
For a stationary wave with a node at each end, the node separation $L = 45 \text{ cm}$ satisfies $L = n\lambda/2$, where $n$ is the number of half-wavelength segments.
Each $\lambda/2$ segment contains exactly one antinode midway between its two nodes, so $n = 3$ means 3 antinodes lie between transmitter and surface. This is option C.
